body_markdown:
In an effort to entice prospective buyers keen on the idea of overlanding in a large vehicle, Ford is rolling out a “this could be you” special edition of its Expedition full-size SUV. It’s called Project Overland, and it looks quite the part.


Ford | Eric Perry


Ford | Eric Perry


The basis for the project was a 2025 model-year Expedition with Ford’s Tremor off-road package, which offers as much as 10.6 inches of ground clearance to start. Then, as with most overland builds, the phone calls started to the aftermarket. Ford designers scooped a set of 17-inch wheels from an[F-150 Raptor R](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/jurassic-park-driving-every-raptor-to-celebrate-15-years-of-madness/) and wrapped them in a set of 35-inch BFGoodrich KO2 all-terrain tires for added grip on the trail.


Ford | Eric Perry


Ford | Eric Perry


Ford | Eric Perry


To help clear those meaty tires, Ford partnered with Fox Factory Vehicles for a 2-inch lift kit and FOX 2.0 Performance Series coilovers. There’s a modified[F-150](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2027-ford-f-150-engine-shuffle-entry-level-off-roaders-a-new-way-to-tow/) bumper up front that houses a hidden Warn winch for particularly hairy situations. Adding a winch up front can substantially reduce the surface area for cooling the engine, though, so Ford’s team fitted this build with an upgraded intercooler that would offset the airflow restrictions.


Ford | Eric Perry


Lighting is just as important as running gear. Project Overland features a set of RIGID Phoenix ditch lights at the base of the A-pillars and a rack of roof lights up top. Speaking of up top: A hallmark of flashy overlanding builds can be aptly described as “a bunch of stuff on your roof,” and Project Overland fits that bill. There’s a Yakima softshell tent and an OverNOut side awning for lodging accommodations, and some recovery boards for when you’re stuck and still working on getting there. Inside, Ford fitted this rig with the overhead console from the F-150 Tremor, which gives you prewired upfitter switches and wireless controls that you can configure to operate bits like the ditch lights and the winch.


Ford | Eric Perry


Ford | Eric Perry


Ford | Eric Perry


All of this is fairly standard stuff for an overlanding build, but it’s interesting to see it fitted to something like the Expedition. To our eyes, we’d guess this is the start of a corporate exploration into how the Blue Oval might further differentiate its largest SUV from the cross-town competition. Ford won’t sell this vehicle as-is, of course; the company is calling it a “test bed” for seeing where it and Fox Factory Vehicles might collaborate next.


ERIC PERRY


If you want to look around the bend, perhaps we’re looking at an options package above the Tremor line in terms of capability. Pure speculation here: perhaps Ford will split the higher-end of the Expedition line into multiple off-road disciplines, bending Tremor more towards higher-speed antics while a second line hews more toward the slower, steadier pace of overlanding. (Toyota has done something similar with the TRD Pro and Trailhunter variants of its[full-size Sequoia](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/toyota-drops-details-on-overlanding-focused-2027-sequoia-trailhunter/) .)


If you want to *really* stretch it, maybe Ford and Fox are covertly working through the early stages of a new model for the Raptor family. After all, it’s Fox that makes the magical suspension systems on all current Raptors. This is an extreme stretch, but it’s also a fun thought exercise.


Project Overland will make its public debut next weekend at the Los Angeles Auto Show. Would you like to see more automakers hop into the overlanding segment?
